proposal.changeSummary: Corrected two factual overreaches in the spine (NEA/videogames exclusion framed as timeless and undated; BLS craft/fine-artist grouping framed as evidence of aesthetic 'significance' rather than administrative convenience with its own preserved distinction), and added fund entries capturing durable clarifications from the exchange: the circulation/consecration distinction sharpened by the Kinkade case, the 'sovereignty over territory vs. map' formulation of art-world authority, the access-to-a-public vs. attention-within-it distinction with platform gatekeeping, and the corrected historical account of the NEA funding retrenchment and videogames' gradual, contested inclusion. No changes made to voice, structure, or proportion beyond these targeted corrections.

entry.title: Circulation versus consecration: what Kinkade's exclusion actually means
entry.markdown: The exclusion at stake in Kinkade's case is institutional and communal, not a verdict on popularity or quality per se. Kinkade was arguably the most circulated painter in America by sales, reproductions, and collectors—he was never excluded from cultural circulation. What excluded him was admission to the specific community that inherited the eighteenth-century invention of art as a transcendent category: the galleries, museums, critics, and academic disciplines that police the term 'art' as a marker of special cultural status. The *Times* obituary's maneuver—displacing appreciation onto Kinkade's self-description and fan tweets rather than the paper's own arts-desk voice—enacts this in miniature: two communities, each with its own standards of value, neither able to impose its terms on the other in full.
entry.useWhen: A reader conflates 'excluded from the art world' with 'excluded from cultural significance or popularity,' or asks what exactly Kinkade was excluded from.

fundOperations.rationale: The exchange (turns 1-2) produces a distinct, durable clarification of a term the spine leaves ambiguous ('excluded'). It sharpens rather than restates the existing argument and is worth preserving for future readers without altering the spine's proportion.

entry.title: Sovereignty over territory, not over the map
entry.markdown: The claim that elite arts are 'no more special than any others' should not be read as claiming the traditional art world's authority has vanished. It retains full control over consecration, museum space, and much of what is taught as art history within its own domain—Kinkade will not enter that curriculum, and prestige (in Van Laar and Diepeveen's sense) remains a real, operating currency there. What has changed is the scope of that authority's claim: it has been demoted from a jurisdiction assumed binding on the culture as a whole (the tacit deference exacted even from those excluded from elite art's enjoyment) to a jurisdiction binding only within its own special interest. The art world has sovereignty over its own territory; it has lost sovereignty over the map.
entry.useWhen: A reader worries that describing art-world authority as diminished implies it has disappeared, or asks whether institutional power over consecration still matters.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 3-4 produce a memorable, precise formulation that qualifies a real symmetry-overstatement risk in the spine's argument (p02, p11) without requiring a spine correction, since the spine itself does not claim art-world authority vanished. This is exactly the kind of durable qualification the fund is for.

entry.title: Access to a public versus attention within it: platform gatekeeping
entry.markdown: Lowering the cost of entering publication is not the same as lowering the cost of being seen once published. A work uploaded to deviantART clears the old barrier of needing an editor, gallery owner, or juried show, but among 251 million uploaded works mere existence is not visibility. Something still sorts the plenitude into what gets attention—now ranking algorithms, tagging conventions, front-page curation, and follower counts rather than critics exercising trained judgment. This is not a return to the old gatekeeping: platform selection does not declare itself as prestige the way named critics and institutions once did, and it is not exclusionary in the same sense (invisible work is not banned, merely unsurfaced). But it is a form of gatekeeping nonetheless, and a less legible one, since it presents itself as neutral aggregation while encoding real biases—toward recency, existing momentum, and whatever the platform is tuned to reward. The durable distinction is not judgment versus popularity (traditional prestige was always entangled with reputation and networking too) but the namability and contestability of the selecting authority: a critic's verdict can be traced to a career and argued with; an algorithm's verdict is diffuse, proprietary, and rarely available for inspection.
entry.useWhen: A reader treats platforms like deviantART as having dissolved gatekeeping entirely, or asks how attention is actually distributed once publication costs fall.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 11-14 develop a genuinely new distinction (access to a public vs. attention within it) that extends the argument about deviantART and platforms in a way the spine does not currently make. This is a durable conceptual development worth preserving as optional material rather than expanding the spine itself, since it is a refinement rather than a correction of an error.

entry.title: Kinkade as transitional case, not exemplary digital-plenitude instance
entry.markdown: The Thomas Kinkade Company's web presence should not be credited with creating an organized, self-sufficient popular public from scratch. Kinkade's enterprise depended on an already fully commercial, hierarchically managed distribution network of branded galleries, independent dealers, and licensing arrangements predating the site (a 2002 SEC filing describes these channels as the company's primary distribution system). This system was substantial, self-financing, and indifferent to art-world sanction well before any website existed; the web presence is continuous with that prior infrastructure rather than its origin. Kinkade therefore sits on the threshold between the older culture-industry model of mass marketing and the plenitude proper. deviantART, by contrast, lacks any equivalent prior organization: its contributors are not funneled through galleries, dealers, or licensing arrangements, and the platform itself is the entire infrastructure of production, distribution, and self-recognition—a productivity (exceeding the Louvre's total holdings every three days) that could not exist in pre-digital form.
entry.useWhen: A reader treats Kinkade's website as the exemplary case of digital plenitude creating a new public, or asks how Kinkade and deviantART differ as evidence for the chapter's claims.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 7-8 supply a specific, sourced historical correction distinguishing Kinkade's pre-existing commercial infrastructure from deviantART's genuinely novel infrastructure. This is a distinct clarification with a real source already supplied in conversation, marked needs-verification because it introduces a specific institutional/historical fact (the SEC filing's characterization) not already established in the spine.

entry.title: Dating the NEA retrenchment and the gradual, uneven inclusion of videogames
entry.markdown: The restriction on NEA funding for experimental performance and installation art should be anchored to a specific mechanism and moment rather than stated as a timeless limit. What was actually curtailed was direct funding for individual artists in these categories following the culture-wars controversies of the late 1980s and early 1990s (the fights over Robert Mapplethorpe, Andres Serrano, and the 'NEA Four' performance artists), which led Congress to eliminate most individual artist grants and impose decency standards on remaining funding. This was a datable, mechanism-specific retrenchment—not a fixed incapacity of the NEA to recognize such work as art—that pushed the boundary outward toward popular forms (gospel, film) while simultaneously pulling it inward against particular formal experimentation, for political rather than aesthetic reasons. Similarly, videogames' exclusion should not be treated as total or permanent: the NEA reported in 2012 that it had encouraged game-related proposals and made grants supporting games, including a game adaptation of Thoreau's *Walden*, and later media-arts materials explicitly include video games. Videogames occupied a genuinely marginal, contested position for a long stretch—treated with the suspicion once directed at film and jazz—and have only gradually, unevenly, and partially been drawn inside the NEA's expanding definition, showing institutional boundary-work happening case by case rather than a settled verdict.
entry.useWhen: A reader treats the NEA's exclusion of experimental art or videogames as a fixed, timeless feature of the institution rather than a datable, contested, and partially renegotiated history.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 17-18 supply a specific, sourced historical correction to the spine's claim about NEA exclusions. Since the correction is substantial and well-supported but the spine's core point (limits on institutional expansion exist) remains valid, the spine itself is being corrected for the absolute framing while this entry preserves the fuller historical detail and source, marked needs-verification as it introduces specific institutional facts and dates.

entry.title: Platforms as new intermediaries, not the absence of intermediation
entry.markdown: Having established that platforms are themselves gatekeeping structures—opaque and algorithmic but structurally real—it would be inconsistent to then describe direct online sales as happening without any institutional intermediary at all. The traditional art-world intermediary (critic, dealer, juried gallery) has indeed been bypassed. But the artist selling through a personal website or social media page depends on a different intermediary: the platform's terms of service, its discovery algorithm, its payment infrastructure. What has changed is which intermediary stands between artist and audience, not whether one exists. The amateur painter who bypasses the art world's institutions becomes dependent instead on a marketplace's search ranking or a feed algorithm—a new, less visible form of mediation replacing the old, more visible one. Likewise, the redistribution of costs that platforms enable (publication, discovery, feedback, affiliation) is not infrastructure-free; it substitutes servers, corporate ownership, and platform governance for the infrastructure of galleries and dealers, continuous with (and accelerating) older amateur traditions like zines, camera clubs, and fan conventions rather than inventing self-organization from nothing.
entry.useWhen: A reader take the chapter's account of digital self-publication to mean artists now operate without any institutional intermediary or infrastructure at all.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 9-10 and 16 together identify and correct a real internal inconsistency in how digital self-publication might be characterized (infrastructure-free vs. redistributed infrastructure). This is a durable qualification that sharpens the argument's precision without requiring alteration of the spine's existing wording, which does not itself make the 'no intermediary at all' claim explicitly.

entry.title: deviantART as a spectrum of aspiration, not a sealed population
entry.markdown: deviantART's contributors are not usefully described as a population sealed off from serious-art discourse, nor is 'most' of that population's relationship to elite art something the case supports characterizing with confidence. An individual contributor may use the platform for peer feedback and fandom while simultaneously pursuing gallery representation, academic credentialing, or festival exhibition under a different professional identity; nothing about the platform's architecture forecloses pursuing platform-native recognition and traditional consecration at once. The defensible claim is narrower and structural: deviantART does not require dialogue with elite art's history as a condition of its own internal system of value. Its favorites, followers, and front-page features constitute a complete, self-referential economy of recognition that functions whether or not any given contributor engages the inherited hierarchy of the traditional art world—deviantART is a limit case of platform-native recognition operating at unprecedented scale and self-sufficiency, not a population external to serious-art discourse. The comparison to Kinkade's aesthetic should likewise specify its terms: a shared visual idiom of highly finished, glowing, idealized imagery that prioritizes emotional warmth and technical smoothness over the disruption or conceptual friction elite criticism has trained itself to value since modernism—a claim about surface aesthetics and address to the viewer, not about the underlying population's relationship to art-world discourse.
entry.useWhen: A reader treats deviantART's contributors as a single, sealed community indifferent to or excluded from elite art discourse, or asks what exactly is meant by comparing deviantART's aesthetics to Kinkade's.

fundOperations.rationale: Turns 19-22 identify and correct a real overstatement (categorical population split, unwarranted 'most,' vague Kinkade comparison) that risks misleading a future reader if left unaddressed, even though it does not rise to a spine-level factual error requiring correction of the authored prose itself. This preserves the refinement as optional supporting material.

spineUpdates.markdown: The American National Endowment for the Arts offers a similar rhetoric that allows popular forms into the canon of art and yet insists that art retains its special role in our culture. The Chairman's Message in the *2012 Guide* tells us that "...[t]he arts are all around us, offering hope, inspiration, and imagination to make us even better, individually and collectively." Given the NEA's funded projects and examples, the arts include gospel singing as well as opera, film and television as well as stage plays. Still the definition does not extend uniformly or without limit throughout the plenitude. Following the culture-wars controversies of the late 1980s and early 1990s, Congress eliminated most individual artist grants and imposed decency standards on remaining funding, a datable retrenchment that made certain kinds of experimental performance and installation art effectively unfundable in that specific category, even as the NEA's definition of art expanded elsewhere. Videogames present a similar story of contested, uneven boundary-work rather than fixed exclusion: for decades they were regarded as too low-brow---either incapable of the range of emotion and expression of art or actually dangerous because they promote violence or other anti-social behavior in their (often adolescent) players---but since the early 2010s the NEA has increasingly encouraged and funded game-related projects, drawing the form gradually and partially inside its expanding definition of art.
spineUpdates.rationale: The reader (turns 17-18) established that the spine's claims about NEA exclusions were materially misleading in their absoluteness: the experimental-art funding restriction is a datable, mechanism-specific consequence of the culture wars rather than a timeless institutional limit, and videogames have since the early 2010s been the subject of active NEA outreach and funding (e.g., the Walden game adaptation), not a fixed exclusion. Per instructions to correct factual statements in the spine shown to be wrong or materially misleading by the exchange, this passage is corrected while preserving its original point about institutional limits and boundary-work.

spineUpdates.markdown: As I write these lines sitting in a cafe in Atlanta, Georgia, I can see on the wall in front of me three paintings in a style vaguely reminiscent of Paul Klee. We have all seen every conceivable style of art serving as interior decoration in business and public buildings. Most of it is mass produced, but some is created by local artists and offered for sale in cafes, restaurants, and malls. This second- or third-tier art reminds us of the large and varied network that has formed in the space between the traditional high art community and the industry that provides decorative art and reproductions for consumers---the space between, say, Gerhard Richter and Thomas Kinkade. The important museums and galleries exhibit artists who have attained an elite status with collectors and critics. Below that level, there are artists who work in more or less the same way: developing a style and exhibiting. They may have exhibitions at less prestigious galleries, and in countries other than the United States, their art may be supported by public funds. At the local level, the exhibitions may be in cafes, where their art is priced in the hundreds rather than the thousands of dollars. This "middle-brow" network allows people with middle-class incomes to collect works in imitation of the elite gallery system. Of course, this description only hints at the complexity of what is regarded as the arts culture today, which includes sales of locally produced arts and crafts of all kinds (from painting and sculpture to pottery and crafts). The Bureau of Labor Statistics website (2017) groups craft and fine artists together for occupational-classification purposes, reporting 50,300 such workers in the workforce in 2014---an administrative convenience rather than a considered verdict on the historical distinction between art and craft, since the agency's own description still distinguishes craft artists' functional objects from fine artists' more purely aesthetic work even while counting them together. But the fact that ordinary labor-market classification finds the line administratively unnecessary to draw says something about how far that distinction has receded in everyday economic life.
spineUpdates.rationale: The reader (turn 15) correctly identified that describing the BLS grouping as evidence that 'says something significant about contemporary culture' overstated the case: the BLS source itself preserves the fine/craft distinction conceptually even while grouping the occupations administratively. This is a materially misleading characterization of a cited source that the spine should not leave uncorrected; the passage is revised to state the more defensible, narrower claim the reader's correction supports.

draftPackage.title: Art as a Special Interest

spine.markdown: The modern category of art has a cultural history that extends back to the eighteenth century, when, as Larry Shiner documented in *The Invention of Art* (2001), art became a special and singularly important form of making. Prior to this time, there had been no universally held distinction between arts and crafts. There were painters, sculptors, poets, architects, and composers, but their callings were not necessarily joined under the term *art*, nor were they necessarily always separated from jewelers, woodworkers, and makers of quilts. After the invention of art, the fine arts became "a matter of inspiration and genius...meant to be enjoyed for themselves in moments of refined pleasure, whereas the crafts and popular arts required only skill and rules and were meant for mere use or entertainment" (Shiner 2001, 5). In the first half of the twentieth century, art still enjoyed this remarkable status. The educated and moneyed elites were able to define what art was, and their definition was deemed to have value for the whole of our culture. Most in the working classes had at best limited access to forms of elite art, but they were still expected tacitly to acknowledge that this elite art performed a central cultural task. In the second half of the twentieth century, the forms of art anointed with the task of saving our culture did not disappear, but they had to learn to coexist with all sorts of popular practices that include popular novels, graphic novels, films, television shows, videogames as well as things that used to be considered hobbies. In one sense, this is a return to an era before art became a transcendent category. Today the gulf between the fine arts and the crafts has narrowed, but now the crafts are not only woodworking and gardening, but also remix audio and video and videogame design. In another sense, of course, the situation is quite different, because the rhetoric of art persists in this postlapsarian era. Jay Z does not want to reduce Picasso to the level of a pop performer; he wants to raise himself to the level of artist.

The elite arts and popular entertainments have all become special interests, each with a community of practitioners and audience. Each may have many subcommunities, and any and all of these can overlap, sharing audience and practitioners. The point is that if elite arts are special interests, they are no more special than any others. No one art has an importance that unarguably transcends its community. This is what the plenitude means for art and indeed other forms of culture today. Each community is still free to define its art as central, and some do, but they cannot make their definition apply universally, as the elites of the nineteenth and earlier twentieth centuries were able to do.

Some communities and audiences are infinitely larger than others. The painter Thomas Kinkade died in 2012, and because of his success in the mass marketing of his work, his web site may be right in claiming that he is America's "Most Collected Artist." He painted in a pseudo-realistic, saccharine style, and his subject matter was usually bucolic scenes of an America that never existed. Kinkade's obituary in the *NY Times* tried to have it both ways (Flegenheimer 2012). It acknowledged Kinkade's success in attracting a vast audience: "Rebelling against what he considered the elitism of modern art, Mr. Kinkade moved his focus to retail, not a traditional gallery system." The article, however, is careful to ascribe appreciations of Kinkade's work to the painter himself ("Kinkade referred to himself as the 'painter of light'") or to fans on Twitter ("'Rest in peace, Thomas Kinkade. May your afterlife be as beautiful as your art.'"). The *Times*'s Arts section now accommodates a variety of communities: from opera and fine art to some kinds of rock music and hip hop, but seldom the enormously popular pop music of say, Justin Bieber or Kelly Clarkson. The changes over the past 60 years in what the *New York Times* chooses to cover in its Arts Section could chart, somewhat belatedly, the breakdown of the great divide between high and popular culture. There is now, for example, a videogames section in the online version of the *New York Times*.

Artistic elites had to contend with the growing importance of popular forms such as film and American jazz throughout the twentieth century, and they dealt with this challenge with a variety of reactions from indignant rejection (Adorno) to conditional acceptance (Benjamin). But the situation is different now. The traditional art community judges Kinkade's painting as the definition of kitsch and as the purest product of the "culture industry," the term still used to describe the machine that markets as commodities pop music, Hollywood film, commercial television, best-selling novels, and so on. But the term only makes sense within the art communities and the academic disciplines affiliated with them. At the same time the vast popularity of a painter like Kinkade does not give his aesthetic any more claim to being at the center of our culture: Kinkade too is a special interest. "Do you like Kinkade?" is now the only kind of question that transcends various communities with their various definitions of art.

As I write these lines sitting in a cafe in Atlanta, Georgia, I can see on the wall in front of me three paintings in a style vaguely reminiscent of Paul Klee. We have all seen every conceivable style of art serving as interior decoration in business and public buildings. Most of it is mass produced, but some is created by local artists and offered for sale in cafes, restaurants, and malls. This second- or third-tier art reminds us of the large and varied network that has formed in the space between the traditional high art community and the industry that provides decorative art and reproductions for consumers---the space between, say, Gerhard Richter and Thomas Kinkade. The important museums and galleries exhibit artists who have attained an elite status with collectors and critics. Below that level, there are artists who work in more or less the same way: developing a style and exhibiting. They may have exhibitions at less prestigious galleries, and in countries other than the United States, their art may be supported by public funds. At the local level, the exhibitions may be in cafes, where their art is priced in the hundreds rather than the thousands of dollars. This "middle-brow" network allows people with middle-class incomes to collect works in imitation of the elite gallery system. Of course, this description only hints at the complexity of what is regarded as the arts culture today, which includes sales of locally produced arts and crafts of all kinds (from painting and sculpture to pottery and crafts). The Bureau of Labor Statistics website (2017) groups craft and fine artists together for occupational-classification purposes, reporting 50,300 such workers in the workforce in 2014---an administrative convenience rather than a considered verdict on the historical distinction between art and craft, since the agency's own description still distinguishes craft artists' functional objects from fine artists' more purely aesthetic work even while counting them together. But the fact that ordinary labor-market classification finds the line administratively unnecessary to draw says something about how far that distinction has receded in everyday economic life.

All this activity goes on as it has for decades in physical galleries and workshops, but it is also vastly amplified by digital forms including websites and other social media pages. Any amateur rock group can have its Facebook or Myspace page and website and sell its music via download. Thomas Kinkade is represented on the web by a complete commercial site (Thomas Kinkade Company 2017) with a gallery (store) locator and an online gallery and shop. Along with such professionally managed sites, there are countless simple sites where individual visual artists display or offer their work for sale. For this network of audiences and outlets, the notions of mass culture and the culture industry no longer seem adequate, if indeed they ever were. The media plenitude today is not just a mass culture industry, but also a myriad of amateurs and vocational artists who fall somewhere between the mass marketing of pop stars and the cloistered markets of traditional art. The multiplication of forms and audiences would not have been possible without the breakdown of the distinction between popular and elite, and it has certainly been fostered by the Web's capacity for easy distribution.

Those who work in or with popular media do not necessarily want the special category of art to be dissolved; instead, they want to see their forms (film, television, graphic novels, or videogames) elevated to something like the status that was enjoyed by the former elite arts. They want to appropriate the term *art* to indicate that their work has the same central cultural mission assigned in the past to elite art. We saw this, for example, in the Jay Z video with which we began. And for decades, film makers, critics, and scholars worked hard to justify film as "serious" art. Because film is the perfect example of the eclectic nature of contemporary media, there are indeed films that can plausibly occupy every level from avant-garde to kitsch. It is not just the works of Eisenstein and Bergman to which the rhetoric of elite art is applied. The American Film Institute promotes the art of film (AFI 2017) and uses all the language of art inherited from modernism. The Academy Awards ceremony each year honors Hollywood films for their artistry, and one of the introducers is bound to say at some point that film shows us "who we are," "presents us with realities we would rather not face," and so on (Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences Web Site 2017).

The American National Endowment for the Arts offers a similar rhetoric that allows popular forms into the canon of art and yet insists that art retains its special role in our culture. The Chairman's Message in the *2012 Guide* tells us that "...[t]he arts are all around us, offering hope, inspiration, and imagination to make us even better, individually and collectively." Given the NEA's funded projects and examples, the arts include gospel singing as well as opera, film and television as well as stage plays. Still the definition does not extend uniformly or without limit throughout the plenitude. Following the culture-wars controversies of the late 1980s and early 1990s, Congress eliminated most individual artist grants and imposed decency standards on remaining funding, a datable retrenchment that made certain kinds of experimental performance and installation art effectively unfundable in that specific category, even as the NEA's definition of art expanded elsewhere. Videogames present a similar story of contested, uneven boundary-work rather than fixed exclusion: for decades they were regarded as too low-brow---either incapable of the range of emotion and expression of art or actually dangerous because they promote violence or other anti-social behavior in their (often adolescent) players---but since the early 2010s the NEA has increasingly encouraged and funded game-related projects, drawing the form gradually and partially inside its expanding definition of art.

Not all digital forms are popular or low-brow in this sense, however. There is a significant digital art community, which sees itself as a part of the larger community of traditional art. Digital artists exhibit at festivals such as *Ars Electronica* and *ISEA*. Many digital artists, who want to be part of the traditional gallery and museum system, complain that their work (installation art with digital components or art that involves the Internet) does not get sufficient recognition beside the traditional media of modern and postmodern art. Nevertheless, these artists do belong to the same community and seem to agree that art has a special cultural status, whether it is appreciated by large audiences or not.

The traditional art community of which digital art yearns to be a part continues to represent a range of economic and social interests. Galleries and auction houses sell paintings of established masters from the Renaissance to the twentieth century for ever higher prices. Museums run blockbuster exhibits (Vermeer, Picasso, da Vinci) that attract thousands of visitors, who are in other ways outside of the community. Contemporary art is represented by such exhibitions as *Documenta* in Germany and the *Venice Biennale*, which are celebrated in the art world and also relatively popular. About a million visitors attended *Documenta 13* in 2012 in the small town of Kassel, and the art exhibited there extends across a large range of contemporary practices. But even if contemporary artists at *Documenta* address political issues ("dOCUMENTA (13) is driven by a holistic and non-logocentric vision that is skeptical of the persisting belief in economic growth") or try to appeal to a broader public, everything about the festival suggests the special (formerly elite) status of art and the artists.

There remains a need for exclusivity in the communities of artists that are heirs to the era before the collapse of hierarchy. Whether we are speaking of the now classic traditions of the galleries and museums (including everything from Renaissance painting to mainstream modernist painters and sculptors), or the contemporary artists who are assimilated into the mainstream (say, David Hockney, Gerhard Richter, or Damien Hirst), or digital artists (whose work and even medium are not yet entirely accepted)---all of these constitute a tacit community for whom the mission of art remains central to culture. They remain in conversation with the elite art of the past. The boundaries of the elite art community have become blurrier in the decades since the 1960s, but there is a vast territory beyond the boundary, where popular and elite practices coexist in every imaginable combination. And precisely because the boundary is now blurred, the art world devotes great energy to deciding what constitutes art as well as what distinguishes good art from poor art. In *Artworld Prestige* (2013), Van Laar and Diepeveen explored prestige as the currency of the art community, particularly for art of the past fifty or so years. Prestige is neither absolute nor eternal; the art community is constantly revising its hierarchy, redrawing its boundaries. The worst thing that can happen to an artist is to lose the brand of seriousness altogether, which moves his or her work definitely beyond the boundary. At the same time, so-called outsider art can be made serious through the work of curators and art critics and then moved inside.

deviantART, a Web site that reflects all the ambiguities and ironies of our culture's current understanding of art, is clearly outside the boundary of the serious art world. The site claims to have 26 million members and 251 million unique works of art (deviantart.theresumator.com 2017). Its production of original art therefore surpasses the total holdings of the Louvre every three days. deviantART constitutes a community (in fact several communities) of those producing various forms of (mostly) visual media. Much of the vast store of works is seamless, glowing 3D illustration, in some ways close to the aesthetics of Thomas Kinkade, but insistent on the medium of the digital rather than paint. But that is only one strand of the universe of deviantART: the site is its own plenitude of possible "expressive" forms. Although the name suggests the historical avant-garde's desire to be disruptive, the majority of the vast membership of contributors are apparently not in dialogue with any of the traditions of elite art.

deviantART suggests the most radically democratic of positions: that art is synonymous with creative expression. This position often emerges in our culture's contemporary rhetoric about art: that everyone can express himself or herself in different ways, that traditional visual art is creative, but so is mathematics, physics, and engineering, and so on. It is common now to say that there is art in each of these scientific or technical practices. Product design is called art (Steve Jobs was an artist, according to his biographer, Walter Isaacson). Traditional crafts are arts. The point is not that this is a misuse of language, as if only the formerly elite arts deserve the name. Our culture has long applied the term *art* in a metaphorical or extended way to these and other practices. The point is rather that, with the collapse of the hierarchy, the term has lost its ability to function as a metaphor. Painting, physics, quilting, product design and chess are all arts in the same way.

A counterpart to deviantART is Artsy (artsy.net). While deviantART uses the Web to publish huge amounts of popular work and insist that these all deserve the name of art, the Artsy website insists that elite art can be popular. Artsy's collections are not user generated; they come from the art community's museums and galleries. Its goal is to make images of Western art available to web users with the same ease and on the same terms as a social media site. When you join the site, you receive a welcoming email that reads: "Our mission is to make all the world's art accessible to anyone with an Internet connection. Discover, learn about, and collect art from the world's top galleries and museums. ...Art is better with friends. You can use this link to share Artsy." And the link invites you to share Artsy through email, Facebook, or Twitter. The email goes on to offer you the opportunity to contact a specialist to help you begin collecting art. Perhaps even more effectively than deviantART, Artsy attests to the dissolving boundary between elite and popular in the realm of art.

The collapse of hierarchy in our culture went beyond art to encompass other forms of sanctioned cultural knowledge. In *Cultural Literacy: What Every American Needs to Know* (1987), E.D. Hirsch and his colleagues argued that Americans, particularly students, had lost a fund of shared knowledge about their culture and history. The book appeared at a time when it still perhaps seemed feasible to shore up and reinstate the hierarchy of knowledge. Hirsch insisted that there were facts, authors, and historical figures that "every American" should know. And Hirsch went on to produce a *Dictionary of Cultural Literacy* and a series of textbooks and to create an organization, The Core Knowledge Foundation, which continues today and has a web presence (Core Knowledge Foundation 2017). In the 1980s Hirsch was criticized (and praised) for his elitist attitude: it was said that he wanted students to know the work of "dead white males." And it is true that his list was heavy with what the humanities counts as knowledge (particularly about literature) and with canonical male authors like Shakespeare and Thoreau. But in a democratizing spirit, he also attempted to canonize popular knowledge from baseball, comic books, Hollywood film, and so on. His argument was a practical and classically American one: that this popular knowledge was needed to read and understand educated discussion in our culture. What Hirsch would not acknowledge was that any such list codifies the standards of a particular community---in this case the community of American academics and writers whose rhetoric by the 1980s included popular as well as classic literary and historical references. Hirsch's work was subsumed into the political debate called the "culture wars," which included the emasculation of the NEA at the end of the twentieth century. Although the culture wars have flared up today, it is on different terms. The culture over which the war was originally fought has long ago become a special interest.

For Hirsch was wrong. There is in practice almost no common cultural ground on which everyone meets, nor do we really expect everyone to meet any more. We can find smart, successful people with any particular ignorance we care to mention: a physicist who cannot name a single rap artist; a rap artist who cannot name a single composer from the nineteenth century; a college student who has never seen a film by Bergman; a construction worker who has never visited an art museum. By the same token, we can find people who break all of these stereotypes: a construction worker who loves Italian opera; a college professor with a passion for skiffle music; a rapper (Jay Z) who collects twentieth-century art. This is precisely the condition of plenitude, in which there is enormous diversity and everyone is free to follow some cultural threads and ignore others.

Shiner (2001) claimed that by the beginning of the nineteenth century the fine arts had been "given [their] transcendent spiritual role of revealing higher truth or healing the soul" and that "this conceptual revolution along with its related institutions still governs our cultural practices" (6). He was wrong in one important respect. From the late eighteenth to the later twentieth century, the institution of art was indeed believed to do the work of salvation for the whole culture. This was clearly the understanding of Schiller, Shelley and Wordsworth, Matthew Arnold, and most of the modernists. Today it is no longer so. Art and its institutions play a vital role only for the arts communities themselves. The rest of our media culture is free to borrow the rhetoric of high art or to ignore it.

fundEntries.title: Circulation versus consecration: what Kinkade's exclusion actually means
fundEntries.markdown: The exclusion at stake in Kinkade's case is institutional and communal, not a verdict on popularity or quality per se. Kinkade was arguably the most circulated painter in America by sales, reproductions, and collectors—he was never excluded from cultural circulation. What excluded him was admission to the specific community that inherited the eighteenth-century invention of art as a transcendent category: the galleries, museums, critics, and academic disciplines that police the term 'art' as a marker of special cultural status. The *Times* obituary's maneuver—displacing appreciation onto Kinkade's self-description and fan tweets rather than the paper's own arts-desk voice—enacts this in miniature: two communities, each with its own standards of value, neither able to impose its terms on the other in full.
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader conflates 'excluded from the art world' with 'excluded from cultural significance or popularity,' or asks what exactly Kinkade was excluded from.

fundEntries.title: Sovereignty over territory, not over the map
fundEntries.markdown: The claim that elite arts are 'no more special than any others' should not be read as claiming the traditional art world's authority has vanished. It retains full control over consecration, museum space, and much of what is taught as art history within its own domain—Kinkade will not enter that curriculum, and prestige (in Van Laar and Diepeveen's sense) remains a real, operating currency there. What has changed is the scope of that authority's claim: it has been demoted from a jurisdiction assumed binding on the culture as a whole (the tacit deference exacted even from those excluded from elite art's enjoyment) to a jurisdiction binding only within its own special interest. The art world has sovereignty over its own territory; it has lost sovereignty over the map.
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader worries that describing art-world authority as diminished implies it has disappeared, or asks whether institutional power over consecration still matters.

fundEntries.title: Access to a public versus attention within it: platform gatekeeping
fundEntries.markdown: Lowering the cost of entering publication is not the same as lowering the cost of being seen once published. A work uploaded to deviantART clears the old barrier of needing an editor, gallery owner, or juried show, but among 251 million uploaded works mere existence is not visibility. Something still sorts the plenitude into what gets attention—now ranking algorithms, tagging conventions, front-page curation, and follower counts rather than critics exercising trained judgment. This is not a return to the old gatekeeping: platform selection does not declare itself as prestige the way named critics and institutions once did, and it is not exclusionary in the same sense (invisible work is not banned, merely unsurfaced). But it is a form of gatekeeping nonetheless, and a less legible one, since it presents itself as neutral aggregation while encoding real biases—toward recency, existing momentum, and whatever the platform is tuned to reward. The durable distinction is not judgment versus popularity (traditional prestige was always entangled with reputation and networking too) but the namability and contestability of the selecting authority: a critic's verdict can be traced to a career and argued with; an algorithm's verdict is diffuse, proprietary, and rarely available for inspection.
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader treats platforms like deviantART as having dissolved gatekeeping entirely, or asks how attention is actually distributed once publication costs fall.

fundEntries.title: Dating the NEA retrenchment and the gradual, uneven inclusion of videogames
fundEntries.markdown: The restriction on NEA funding for experimental performance and installation art should be anchored to a specific mechanism and moment rather than stated as a timeless limit. What was actually curtailed was direct funding for individual artists in these categories following the culture-wars controversies of the late 1980s and early 1990s (the fights over Robert Mapplethorpe, Andres Serrano, and the 'NEA Four' performance artists), which led Congress to eliminate most individual artist grants and impose decency standards on remaining funding. This was a datable, mechanism-specific retrenchment—not a fixed incapacity of the NEA to recognize such work as art—that pushed the boundary outward toward popular forms (gospel, film) while simultaneously pulling it inward against particular formal experimentation, for political rather than aesthetic reasons. Similarly, videogames' exclusion should not be treated as total or permanent: the NEA reported in 2012 that it had encouraged game-related proposals and made grants supporting games, including a game adaptation of Thoreau's *Walden*, and later media-arts materials explicitly include video games. Videogames occupied a genuinely marginal, contested position for a long stretch—treated with the suspicion once directed at film and jazz—and have only gradually, unevenly, and partially been drawn inside the NEA's expanding definition, showing institutional boundary-work happening case by case rather than a settled verdict.
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader treats the NEA's exclusion of experimental art or videogames as a fixed, timeless feature of the institution rather than a datable, contested, and partially renegotiated history.

fundEntries.title: deviantART as a spectrum of aspiration, not a sealed population
fundEntries.markdown: deviantART's contributors are not usefully described as a population sealed off from serious-art discourse, nor is 'most' of that population's relationship to elite art something the case supports characterizing with confidence. An individual contributor may use the platform for peer feedback and fandom while simultaneously pursuing gallery representation, academic credentialing, or festival exhibition under a different professional identity; nothing about the platform's architecture forecloses pursuing platform-native recognition and traditional consecration at once. The defensible claim is narrower and structural: deviantART does not require dialogue with elite art's history as a condition of its own internal system of value. Its favorites, followers, and front-page features constitute a complete, self-referential economy of recognition that functions whether or not any given contributor engages the inherited hierarchy of the traditional art world—deviantART is a limit case of platform-native recognition operating at unprecedented scale and self-sufficiency, not a population external to serious-art discourse. The comparison to Kinkade's aesthetic should likewise specify its terms: a shared visual idiom of highly finished, glowing, idealized imagery that prioritizes emotional warmth and technical smoothness over the disruption or conceptual friction elite criticism has trained itself to value since modernism—a claim about surface aesthetics and address to the viewer, not about the underlying population's relationship to art-world discourse.
fundEntries.useWhen: A reader treats deviantART's contributors as a single, sealed community indifferent to or excluded from elite art discourse, or asks what exactly is meant by comparing deviantART's aesthetics to Kinkade's.

draftPackage.changeSummary: Corrected two factual overreaches in the spine (NEA/videogames exclusion framed as timeless and undated; BLS craft/fine-artist grouping framed as evidence of aesthetic 'significance' rather than administrative convenience with its own preserved distinction), and added fund entries capturing durable clarifications from the exchange: the circulation/consecration distinction sharpened by the Kinkade case, the 'sovereignty over territory vs. map' formulation of art-world authority, the access-to-a-public vs. attention-within-it distinction with platform gatekeeping, and the corrected historical account of the NEA funding retrenchment and videogames' gradual, contested inclusion. No changes made to voice, structure, or proportion beyond these targeted corrections. Validation: Approve both spine corrections (NEA/videogames dating and mechanism; BLS grouping reframed as administrative convenience that preserves the conceptual distinction) as genuine, well-supported improvements to the authoritative route. Of the seven proposed fund entries, approve five as accepted/candidate additions that capture durable, nonduplicative clarifications supported by the exchange; reject the Kinkade-SEC-filing entry because it introduces a specific, unsupplied external factual claim (SEC filing characterization) as though load-bearing for a historical distinction, better handled as a lighter-weight qualification without over-relying on an unverified primary document read into the record only via a bare link; and reject the platform-as-new-intermediary entry as substantially duplicative of the access-vs-attention entry, restating the same 'platforms are gatekeepers/intermediaries too' point without enough distinct content to justify a separate fund slot.
